title: Great Leaders Know When to Let It Burn Leadership The Business Leader Daily
author: The Business Leader Daily
summary: This issue argues that the defining leadership discipline is not firefighting skill but fire triage: distinguishing which fires genuinely require the leader's attention and which will burn out, resolve themselves, or be handled by those closer to the problem. The central claim is that noise is rarely a signal of importance, and that confusing urgency with impact is one of the most expensive mistakes a leader can make. The article assembles a battery of supporting voices -- Drucker on efficient non-work, Covey on scheduling priorities, Barra and Nadella on problem selection, Arnaud Chevallier on how 60% of executives cite poor problem formulation as a barrier to effective problem-solving. The practical reframe: focus is not what you spend time on but what you refuse to spend time on; great leaders build an impact filter rather than an urgency filter.
points: Urgency is a terrible filter for leadership attention: squeaky wheels demand grease by design, but noise is rarely a signal of importance, and treating every loud problem as equally urgent is one of the most expensive mistakes a leader makes.

The discipline of strategic focus is a discipline of refusal: every yes to a low-impact request is an implicit no to something larger, and most leaders understand this in theory while failing to hold the line in practice.

The reactive leader fights every fire equally; the disciplined leader stops to ask 'what happens if I do nothing here?' -- and more often than not, the honest answer is that the fire resolves itself or belongs to someone closer to it.

Chevallier's research across 700 international executives found that 60% cited poor problem formulation as a top barrier to effective problem-solving -- leaders are spending significant energy solving the wrong problems, not the right ones badly.

Great leaders are not better firefighters -- they are better at deciding which fires deserve a firefighter at all, which requires building an organizational culture that identifies the 'right boulder' rather than rewarding frantic activity.
quotes: Not All Fires Are Equal. A loud complaint from a vocal stakeholder can pull you in for a week, while the strategic question that will define your future sits untouched. Squeaky wheels demand grease. They are noisy by design. But noise is rarely a signal of importance, and confusing the two is one of the most expensive mistakes a leader can make.

Focus is not what you spend your time on. Focus is what you refuse to spend your time on. Every yes to a low-impact request is a no to something larger. Most leaders understand this in theory. Few hold the line in practice.
'There is nothing so useless as doing efficiently that which should not be done at all.' -- Peter F. Drucker

'In our study of more than 700 international executives, 60% identified poor problem formulation as one of the two most prevalent barriers to effective problem-solving in their organizations.' -- Arnaud Chevallier
Great leaders are not better firefighters. They are better at deciding which fires deserve a firefighter at all.

'I spoke with one CEO who said that, in each of the last three companies he had run, he had started by getting the teams focused on the right boulder. Interestingly, in all three cases, the team's previous focus had been on something extra -- ancillary businesses or acquisitions -- and this CEO led them to refocus on the health of the core business.' -- Dan Heath
